War by Feeling, Government by Template

As the Iran conflict spread economic pain and strained alliances, courts pushed back on the administration's vaccine, media, and voter-data campaigns while a senior security official resigned in protest

```markdown This was a week defined by two collisions: an undeclared war run on instinct rather than strategy, and a federal government repeatedly overreaching into courtrooms, statehouses, and newsrooms, only to be checked—sometimes forcefully—by judges, senators, and its own internal dissenters. By week's end, gas lines were lengthening, a career national security official had resigned in protest, and courts had blocked or questioned no fewer than five separate executive actions. Little of it resolved cleanly. Most of it simply hardened into precedent.

**The Weekend**

The tone was set early. Energy Secretary Chris Wright invoked Defense Production Act authority—a Cold War-era statute meant for wartime industrial mobilization—to force the reopening of an offshore oil pipeline in Santa Ynez, California, shuttered since a 2015 spill under a court-approved settlement. The pipeline began shipping oil within days, brushing aside state environmental law and prompting Governor Newsom to threaten suit. It was an early marker of a week in which federal power would repeatedly override negotiated legal arrangements rather than work within them.

Abroad, the war with Iran continued to defy conventional description. Trump told reporters the conflict would end "when I feel it in my bones," resisting any articulation of strategy or objectives. Reporting surfaced that he had waved off warnings from the Joint Chiefs chairman that striking Iran would trigger closure of the Strait of Hormuz—warnings that proved accurate almost immediately, catching the administration flat-footed as global oil markets convulsed. At home, that credibility gap collided with rising pressure on the press: Defense Secretary Hegseth publicly griped about unflattering war coverage and floated a Trump-friendly buyer for CNN, while FCC Chair Brendan Carr threatened broadcasters with license revocation over what he called "hoaxes and news distortions." Separately, Jared Kushner, still functioning as an Iran policy envoy, was soliciting at least $5 billion in fresh investment from Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the UAE—the same governments lobbying him on the war—despite having pledged not to raise capital during his father-in-law's presidency. And in Texas, nine defendants were convicted on material-support-for-terrorism charges over a 2025 protest at an ICE facility, the first federal prosecution to allege that demonstrators belonged to an antifa terrorist cell, with sentences reaching life imprisonment.

Immigration enforcement, meanwhile, produced its own quiet emergencies: a Canadian citizen and her autistic seven-year-old daughter, both legally documented, were detained at a Texas checkpoint and pressured to self-deport; a federal judge ordered the release of an asylum seeker held 50 days in defiance of a court order barring his removal; and a 3,000-agent DHS operation in Minneapolis, the largest of its kind, ended with two U.S. citizens fatally shot.

**Monday**

The week's institutional battles came into sharper focus. The Justice Department's demand for unredacted voter rolls from all fifty states—and its lawsuits against five that refused—collapsed under an avalanche of its own errors: nonexistent statutes cited in court filings, misspelled attorney names, states misidentified as commonwealths, internal drafting notes left in public documents, and complaints struck by judges for procedural violations. Maine, Minnesota, New Hampshire, and West Virginia refused to comply; roughly a dozen states, including Ohio, did. It was a campaign that raised as many questions about competence as about intent.

The same day, Trump signed an executive order creating a Task Force to Eliminate Fraud with sweeping authority over Medicaid, SNAP, and other state-run programs, then directed it to investigate Rep. Ilhan Omar based on false citizenship claims, accompanied by disparaging remarks about Somalia. Courts pushed back hard: Judge Brian Murphy blocked RFK Jr.'s wholesale replacement of the vaccine advisory committee, ruling it likely violated federal law and halting changes to the childhood immunization schedule. Trump, for his part, responded to the Supreme Court's earlier rejection of his tariffs not by retreating but by reimposing them under a different statute, while publicly attacking the Court and demanding it validate his false 2020 election claims.

In a smaller but telling moment, Trump disclosed a sitting congressman's terminal medical diagnosis at a press conference without consent, prompting an immediate objection from Speaker Johnson; the congressman later announced his retirement. The press-freedom pressure from the weekend escalated further as Trump said he was "thrilled" the FCC was reviewing broadcast licenses and called for treason charges against unfavorable outlets. Immigration enforcement continued to generate grim data points—a 19-year-old's death in ICE custody in Florida, one of at least ten detention deaths in 2026, and a report showing ICE arrests of Asian Americans had nearly quadrupled compared to the prior administration.

**Tuesday**

Tuesday brought the week's most consequential act of internal dissent. Joe Kent, director of the National Counterterrorism Center, resigned, stating plainly that Iran posed no imminent threat and that the war had been driven by Israeli pressure rather than U.S. intelligence findings. Trump's response was immediate and public: he dismissed Kent as "weak on security," called him "just the coffee boy," and made clear that dissenters had no place on his team. The episode would escalate further as the week went on.

Separately, Trump claimed he could withdraw from NATO without congressional approval, a claim a fellow Republican publicly corrected as contrary to statute. The House Oversight Committee subpoenaed Attorney General Bondi to testify under oath about the DOJ's handling of Epstein-related files, and Chief Justice Roberts, without naming Trump directly, warned in a public address that attacks on judges were "dangerous" and needed to stop—a rare institutional alarm sounded amid rising threats against the judiciary. Speaker Johnson, meanwhile, declined to hold public hearings on the war's costs, calling the operations too sensitive and describing Trump's "feel it in my bones" approach as a legitimate gut decision informed by intelligence.

Trump simultaneously pressured Republican senators over the Save America Act, an expansive voter-eligibility bill critics warned could disenfranchise up to 21 million voters, threatening to withhold endorsements and demanding the filibuster's elimination to pass it. Immigration cases added further texture: a legally documented Texas court interpreter was detained for over a month without explanation, and pro-Palestinian activist Leqaa Kordia was released after a year in custody despite three judicial findings that she posed no threat.

**Wednesday**

Wednesday was the week's heaviest day for testimony and judicial rebuke. FBI Director Kash Patel admitted under oath that the bureau purchases Americans' location data from commercial brokers without a warrant, drawing bipartisan criticism, including from Republican Rep. Warren Davidson, who called it a Fourth Amendment violation. Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard's written statement asserted Iran's nuclear program had been "obliterated," but she omitted the claim in person and told senators only the president determines what counts as an imminent threat—directly at odds with the intelligence community's own March 2025 assessment that Iran was not building a weapon.

Judge Royce Lamberth ordered the reinstatement of more than a thousand Voice of America employees, ruling the administration's dismantling of the outlet unlawful and setting a March 23 deadline for a restoration plan. Attorney General Bondi, rather than complying with her subpoena, appeared at a closed-door, unsworn briefing; when she declined to commit to sworn testimony, Democratic committee members walked out. Separately, Judge Richard Leon called Trump's $400 million White House ballroom project "brazen" and signaled he might halt it outright.

Amid escalating war costs, Federal Reserve data showed producer prices rising at their fastest pace in a year, and White House economic advisor Kevin Hassett drew bipartisan condemnation for saying consumers were "the last of our concerns." In a smaller but revealing detail, White House communications staff produced "banger meme" videos splicing military strikes with football highlights and movie clips, aimed at young online audiences.

**Thursday**

Thursday brought the formal congressional reckoning with the war, and it did not go well for oversight advocates. The Senate voted 53–47, almost entirely along party lines, to block a Democratic resolution requiring congressional authorization for the ongoing conflict, even as strikes had by then killed more than 1,300 Iranians and hundreds of Lebanese civilians; only Rand Paul crossed party lines. In testimony that day, Senator Ossoff pressed Gabbard further, establishing on the record that the intelligence community itself had not assessed Iran as an imminent threat, and accused her of evading questions to protect White House messaging.

Elsewhere, a New York Times investigation into decades of alleged sexual abuse by labor leader Cesar Chavez triggered a rapid cascade of institutional responses: within a day, Arizona discontinued its Chavez Day holiday, the AFL-CIO withdrew its endorsement, and the United Farm Workers and LUPE canceled planned celebrations.

Reporting also documented systematic failures in deportation practice, with interviews of over a thousand deportees to Honduras revealing that ICE officers routinely failed to ask about children or arrange care before removal, violating the administration's own weakened family-separation directive; separately, a federal judge denied asylum to a five-year-old facing expedited removal. Courts continued to push back elsewhere: a First Circuit panel dismissed lawsuits alleging that pro-Palestinian protest slogans violated civil-rights law, and a federal judge ruled that RFK Jr. had exceeded his authority in restricting gender-affirming care for minors.

Senator Wyden accused Deputy Attorney General Blanche of blocking release of an unclassified Epstein-related memo to Congress, calling it part of a "continued coverup." And Treasury Secretary Bessent floated easing sanctions on stranded Iranian oil to relieve price pressure, even as the International Energy Agency declared the Strait of Hormuz closure the worst supply disruption in the history of the global oil market.

**Friday**

The week closed with more of the same institutional patterns settling into place rather than resolving. Republican leaders permitted only closed-door briefings on the war, with Senator Ron Johnson arguing that public division would undermine the war effort, and a second Democratic attempt to force congressional authorization was again rejected. The Senate Homeland Security Committee advanced Markwayne Mullin's nomination for DHS Secretary on a near party-line vote, with Democrat John Fetterman providing the deciding vote despite unresolved concerns about Mullin's truthfulness and past comments on political violence; Rand Paul, who had raised those same concerns days earlier, dissented.

The Justice Department formally invoked privilege to block release of the Epstein-related DEA memo, dismissing the House Oversight subpoena as "completely unnecessary" while acknowledging that roughly 200,000 pages remained withheld on similar grounds. And the earlier terrorism conviction of anti-ICE protesters widened into a broader pattern, as federal prosecutors filed conspiracy charges against demonstrators in Chicago, investigated Minnesota's governor and Minneapolis's mayor on the same theory, and charged two journalists who had been covering a protest. The week's final small note was almost fitting: Trump misrepresented a CNN poll, claiming 100 percent support for the war when the figure in fact reflected only MAGA Republicans, a group in which other polling showed meaningful dissent.

Taken as a whole, the week showed a presidency willing to act first and litigate the consequences later—overriding state law, reshuffling expert panels, demanding voter data, and reimposing tariffs after judicial rejection—while Congress, controlled by the president's own party, declined at nearly every turn to exercise the oversight authority the Constitution assigns it, whether over war-making, spending, or executive testimony. The judiciary emerged as the most consistent counterweight, reinstating fired broadcasters, blocking a reconstituted health panel, and questioning a quarter-billion-dollar construction project on federal historic ground. But courts move case by case, and much of what happened this week—a war conducted by feeling, a senior official pushed out for stating an inconvenient fact, and prosecutions reaching further into protest and journalism than before—will not be undone by any single ruling. It was a week that tested, in concrete and mostly measurable ways, how much institutional friction still stands between executive will and its exercise. ```
